title: Functor
body:
A container you can map a function over without disturbing its shape. One operation:

```haskell
class Functor f where
    fmap :: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b
```

Read `f` as the container and the signature as: given a function on elements, get a function on
containers. The `f` stays `f` on both sides, and that is the content of the idea, **the
structure is preserved and only the contents change.**

```haskell
fmap (* 2) [1, 2, 3]        -- [2, 4, 6]        a list of three stays a list of three
fmap (* 2) (Just 5)         -- Just 10
fmap (* 2) Nothing          -- Nothing          no value to touch, shape unchanged
fmap (* 2) (Node l 3 r)     -- the same tree with every label doubled
```

The `Nothing` case is the one that shows why this is worth naming. You did not write a null
check; `fmap` had nothing to apply the function to, so it returned the same shape. The
[[Algebraic Data Type|`Maybe`]] handling is in the instance, once, rather than at every call
site.

## The laws

An instance is only a functor if it obeys two equations, and they say exactly "does not disturb
the shape":

$$\texttt{fmap id} = \texttt{id} \qquad\qquad \texttt{fmap (g . h)} = \texttt{fmap g . fmap h}$$

The first forbids an instance that reverses the list or drops elements while mapping. The
second says mapping twice is mapping once with the composition, which is what licenses the
compiler's `map` fusion optimisation. Neither is checked by the compiler; they are proof
obligations on whoever writes the instance, discharged by the equational reasoning in
[[Program Correctness]].

These are the [[Category Theory]] functor laws unchanged: preserve identities, preserve
composition. That is not an analogy, it is the same definition read in the category of Haskell
types.

## The ladder

`Functor` is the bottom rung of the [[Type Class]] hierarchy that ends at [[Monad]], and the
three rungs answer three increasingly hard questions:

| Class | Operation | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `Functor` | `fmap :: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b` | apply a **plain** function inside |
| `Applicative` | `<*> :: f (a -> b) -> f a -> f b` | apply a **wrapped** function to a wrapped value |
| [[Monad]] | `>>= :: m a -> (a -> m b) -> m b` | apply a function that **returns a wrapped value** |

Each rung requires the one below it. The distinction that actually matters is at the top: with
`fmap` and `<*>` the structure of the computation is fixed before it runs, while `>>=` lets the
next step *depend on* the previous result. Applicative is enough for "validate these three
fields independently"; only a monad can express "read the file named in the config".

## Core Facts to Know

- `fmap :: (a -> b) -> f a -> f b`: map a function over a structure, preserving the structure.
- Laws: `fmap id = id`, and `fmap (g . h) = fmap g . fmap h`.
- The laws are the [[Category Theory]] functor laws, unchanged.
- They are not compiler-checked; they are obligations on the instance author.
- `fmap` over `Nothing` is `Nothing`: the null check lives in the instance, not the call site.
- `<$>` is the infix spelling of `fmap`.
- [[Functor]] → `Applicative` → [[Monad]] is a hierarchy, each requiring the last.
- Only [[Monad]] lets a later step depend on an earlier step's *value*.
